summary:
The Pitcairn Islands stand under the United Kingdom's framework: defence and external affairs are reserved to the United Kingdom, and United Kingdom domestic measures such as the Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not apply here of their own force. Local law governs, and those measures could reach Pitcairn only by Order in Council.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Pitcairn Islands since 2001, so a visitor faces no criminalisation exposure on that ground.

The Pitcairn Constitution Order 2010 prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, and that guarantee has been in force since 2010. It is a constitutional protection rather than an offence provision, and it names sexual orientation rather than gender identity.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 14 May 2015. The Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance 2015 defines marriage as the union of two people regardless of sex, sexual orientation or gender identity, and it recognises civil partnerships performed outside Pitcairn. The Island Council approved the ordinance unanimously on 1 April 2015, Governor Jonathan Sinclair signed it on 5 May 2015, and it was published on 13 May 2015.

Adoption has been legal since 2015 and is open to married, unmarried and single people.
tangentialFactors:
Military service in the Pitcairn Islands falls under United Kingdom responsibility rather than local authority, so any service-related question sits with the United Kingdom.

The territory is indexed within United Kingdom LGBT-rights timelines by the source material, which reflects the constitutional link rather than the application of United Kingdom domestic statutes locally.

Population scale shapes practical exposure: roughly 50 residents live across the territory, and none of them is known to be in a same-sex relationship. A visitor's visibility in a small community is therefore governed more by local familiarity than by any documented pattern of same-sex couples on the island.
localsOnly:
Residents are covered by the anti-discrimination guarantee in the Pitcairn Constitution Order 2010, which has protected against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation since 2010.

Local residents may marry without regard to sex, sexual orientation or gender identity under the Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance 2015, and civil partnerships entered into outside Pitcairn are recognised. Adoption is available to married, unmarried and single people under the arrangements in force since 2015.

Local law is the operative law for these matters; United Kingdom measures apply only if extended by Order in Council.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory is silent on gender-marker change procedures, on recognition of documents issued in a visitor's affirmed gender, and on any screening at the point of entry. Nothing in the inventory establishes either a permissive or a restrictive position on those questions, and they remain unresolved here.

Whether the sexual-orientation guarantee in the 2010 Constitution Order extends to gender identity, and whether any hate-crime or aggravated-offence provision covers anti-trans conduct, is not sourced and is left open.

No source records enforcement activity, complaint outcomes under the constitutional guarantee, or any incident of violence against a trans visitor or resident. The absence of such records in this inventory is not evidence that none exists.

Access to gender-affirming healthcare, eligibility rules for such care, and the position on sterilisation or medical requirements are not covered by any source supplied for this dossier.
